title: QuadTok: Quadtree Visual Tokenizer for Autoregressive Image Generation

paper.title: QuadTok: Quadtree Visual Tokenizer for Autoregressive Image Generation
paper.abstract: Abstract We introduce QuadTok, a novel framework for visual tokenization and autoregressive image generation. Compared to traditional approaches using 2D grids or 1D token sequences, we propose a hierarchical quadtree structure, bridging the gap between 2D spatial binding and 1D sequence-level flexibility. The QuadTok tokenizer dynamically allocates representational capacity to visually intricate areas while leaving homogeneous regions at a coarse resolution. Compared with a fixed 256-token grid, our ImageNet-trained tokenizer saves approximately 10% of tokens on ImageNet and 9% when transferred zero-shot to COCO dataset, while maintaining comparable reconstruction fidelity. Furthermore, the natural causality introduced by the tree structure seamlessly enables autoregressive image generation. Conditioned on a quadtree topology supplied before generation, our 947M GPT-style generative model achieves a 2.08 gFID on the ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 benchmark. Additionally, leveraging the strong spatial correlation preserved by the quadtree structure, the QuadTok generator enables zero-shot spatially controlled image generation capabilities. Code: https://github.com/myc634/QuadTok .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Natural images exhibit highly non-uniform spatial information density: regions containing intricate textures and high-frequency patterns carry significantly more information than smooth or homogeneous areas. Ideally, a visual tokenizer should allocate representational capacity according to this spatial variability. However, classic visual tokenizers ( van den Oord et al., 2018 ; Sun et al., 2024 ) compress images into rigid 2D grids with a fixed token budget, distributing tokens uniformly across the image regardless of local complexity. As a result, complex regions are often under-represented while simple regions are over-allocated with redundant tokens. To overcome the rigidity of grid-based tokenization, recent work has explored 1D visual tokenizers ( Shen et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2024b ; Duggal et al., 2024 ; Miwa et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Bachmann et al., 2025b ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . These methods model images as sequential token streams and allow for variable length, offering greater flexibility in adapting the token budget to image complexity. Nevertheless, this flexibility comes at the cost of spatial awareness. Because token allocation occurs along the sequence dimension rather than the image plane, these approaches remain largely spatially agnostic. Consequently, they often lack explicit correspondence between tokens and image patches, which can degrade pixel-level fidelity and make them less suitable for downstream tasks that require spatially grounded representations and precise localization. In this work, we propose QuadTok , a novel quadtree-based visual tokenizer that enables adaptive token allocation while preserving explicit spatial correspondence. Instead of relying on a rigid grid or a purely sequential representation, QuadTok represents images using a hierarchical quadtree structure that dynamically subdivides spatial regions based on local complexity. This design bridges the gap between existing paradigms: it retains the spatial grounding of traditional 2D tokenizers while introducing the sequence-level flexibility of 1D token representations. However, one key challenge remains: How can we select which regions to refine based on their reconstruction benefit? To tackle this, we propose Region-Wise Complexity Guidance , a data-driven strategy to select a content-adaptive tree for each image based on reconstruction benefit. Furthermore, we identify that maintaining the hierarchical causality and explicit spatial relationships between tree nodes is crucial during the tokenization process. To enforce this structural integrity, we introduce the Kinship Causal Mask . This mechanism dictates a strict coarse-to-fine information flow along the quadtree hierarchy, allowing the global image structure to be established before localized refinement occurs within spatially bounded regions. Empowered by our Region-Wise Complexity Guidance , the QuadTok tokenizer achieves an rFID of 1.46 and a PSNR of 20.37 on ImageNet with 230 tokens on average, saving approximately 10% relative to a fixed 256-token grid. Transferred zero-shot to COCO, the same tokenizer uses 232 tokens on average, saving approximately 9%. Furthermore, leveraging the causality inherent in the quadtree structure, the QuadTok 947M autoregressive generator achieves a gFID of 2.08, compared with 2.15 for the 1.4B RandAR-XXL model ( Pang et al., 2025 ) . We also show a consistent scaling behavior on our generator across different model scales. Furthermore, guided by the explicit quadtree topology, QuadTok generator enables novel zero-shot capabilities such as spatially controllable generation. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose QuadTok , a quadtree-based visual tokenizer that replaces fixed-grid representations with spatially adaptive token allocation. Our approach preserves explicit spatial correspondence while enabling flexible token budgets driven by local visual complexity. • We introduce two key mechanisms to support adaptive tokenization: (i) Region-Wise Complexity Guidance strategy selecting regional refinement from reconstruction benefit; (ii) a Kinship Causal Mask enforcing hierarchical dependencies among tree nodes during tokenization. • Leveraging the hierarchical causality of quadtrees, QuadTok achieves competitive image generation quality while enabling zero-shot spatially controllable image synthesis conditioned on quadtree layouts supplied before generation.

sections.heading: 2.1 Visual Tokenization
sections.text: Visual tokenizers compress images into representations for generative modeling. VQ-VAE ( van den Oord et al., 2018 ) learns discrete codebooks, and VQ-GAN ( Esser et al., 2021 ) adds adversarial training to improve perceptual reconstruction. Later work improves codebook design and tokenizer architectures ( Lee et al., 2022 ; Mentzer et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2024a ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) . Beyond fixed spatial grids, TiTok ( Yu et al., 2024b ) represents images as compact 1D sequences. FlexTok ( Bachmann et al., 2025a ) and One-D-Piece ( Miwa et al., 2025b ) support variable sequence lengths, while GigaTok ( Xiong et al., 2025 ) uses semantic regularization to improve reconstruction and downstream generation as tokenizers scale. QuadTok focuses on assigning discrete tokens to regions within an image while retaining an explicit spatial correspondence.

sections.heading: Content-adaptive tokenization.
sections.text: CAT ( Shen et al., 2025 ) adapts representation capacity to image complexity by using caption-derived scores to select an image-wide compression ratio in a nested continuous VAE. Its variable-length latents support image synthesis with a diffusion transformer. QuadTok instead allocates discrete tokens at different spatial resolutions within each image, preserving explicit correspondence between tokens and regions. During reconstruction, image content determines which regions to refine; during generation, an autoregressive model predicts visual codes under a topology supplied before sampling. We compare with CAT’s published ImageNet 512 × 512 512\times 512 generation results in Tab. 7 , alongside other high-resolution generators.

sections.heading: 2.2 Autoregressive Image Generation
sections.text: Autoregressive image models differ in both their latent representation and prediction unit ( Lee et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Shan et al., 2026 ) . LlamaGen ( Sun et al., 2024 ) predicts discrete grid tokens sequentially, RandAR ( Pang et al., 2025 ) changes their generation order, and VAR ( Tian et al., 2024 ) predicts successive resolution scales. DPAR ( Srivastava et al., 2025 ) uses an entropy model to group discrete tokens into variable-length patches, reducing the sequence processed by its global transformer. We compare with DPAR as a related approach to spatial token aggregation. QuadTok represents regions directly as quadtree nodes and generates their discrete codes in breadth-first order conditioned on the given tree. Continuous-token methods provide another approach to autoregressive synthesis. xAR ( Ren et al., 2025a ) generalizes the prediction unit to entities such as cells and uses flow matching with noisy contexts. FlowAR ( Ren et al., 2025b ) combines scale-wise autoregression with flow matching. QuadTok models variable-length discrete sequences with explicit regional correspondence, allowing generation to be conditioned on a supplied spatial topology.

sections.heading: 2.3 Quadtree Representations in Vision
sections.text: Quadtrees recursively partition two-dimensional space and have been used for image processing, compression, and adaptive visual computation ( Wu, 2018 ; Tang et al., 2022 ; Ronen et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) . QuadTok incorporates this hierarchy into a generative visual tokenizer. Its topology-aware attention preserves structured interactions among tokens, and its discrete representation supports image reconstruction and autoregressive synthesis under a supplied spatial topology.

sections.heading: 3.1 QuadTok Tokenizer
sections.text: We introduce QuadTok, a visual tokenizer that represents images using an adaptive quadtree structure. Unlike conventional methods that rely on fixed grids, QuadTok dynamically allocates tokens across regions while maintaining explicit correspondence between tokens and the image patches.

sections.heading: 3.1.1 Quadtree Representation
sections.text: QuadTok represents an image using a hierarchical quadtree decomposition, where each node corresponds to a spatial region and is treated as a visual token. A node is defined by the attribute tuple ( l , p ) (l,p) , where l l denotes the tree level and p p the spatial index. Level l = 1 l=1 represents coarse regions of the image, while level l = 2 l=2 corresponds to higher-resolution subdivisions. Each parent node may expand into four child nodes covering its spatial quadrants. Our default configuration uses two levels; we also evaluate a three-level extension in Secs. 4.1 and 4.2. To interface this hierarchical structure with Transformer architecture, the quadtree is serialized into a 1D sequence using breadth-first search (BFS) traversal. This ordering first lists all coarse tokens and then their corresponding higher-resolution child tokens, naturally aligning with coarse-to-fine generation.

The discrete tokens are first mapped back to continuous embeddings using the codebook and combined with their corresponding structural instruction embeddings. sections.heading: 3.1.5 Tree-Structure Sampling
sections.text: Although the tokenizer can operate on arbitrary quadtree structures, training with a fixed fully expanded tree would cause the model to rely on a deterministic token layout. To improve robustness to variable tree structures, we employ a probabilistic tree sampling strategy during training. Instead of always using a fully expanded quadtree, we randomly sample valid subtrees for each training iteration. All level- 1 1 nodes are always retained to preserve the global image layout, while each parent node independently expands into its four child nodes with probability γ \gamma . When a parent node is not expanded, its spatial region remains represented solely by the coarse-level token. This stochastic sampling exposes the tokenizer to diverse tree configurations and sequence lengths during training. As a result, the model learns to produce consistent representations under both coarse and refined token layouts, enabling it to robustly process the adaptive tree structures used during complexity-guided tokenization (to be introduced in Sec. 3.3 ).

sections.heading: 3.2 Kinship Causal Attention
sections.text: Flattening the quadtree into a 1D sequence removes the explicit hierarchical constraints of the original structure. Without additional restrictions, standard self-attention would allow tokens to interact globally, potentially breaking the spatial correspondence between tokens and their associated image regions. To preserve the hierarchical topology, we introduce Kinship Causal Attention , a topology-aware masking strategy that constrains attention according to the quadtree structure. During encoding, the Aggregator Transformer processes the concatenated sequence [ F ∥ Q ] [F\parallel Q] of ViT feature tokens F F and quadtree instruction tokens Q Q . Attention is asymmetric: ViT tokens attend bidirectionally among themselves, and quadtree tokens attend to all ViT tokens, but not vice versa. Tree tokens thus draw on globally contextualized image features, while their region and level embeddings specify the regions they represent. During decoding, the Decoder Transformer processes the quantized visual tokens together with their corresponding quadtree instruction tokens. In both the encoding and decoding stages, the self-attention interactions among quadtree tokens are governed by our proposed Kinship Causal Mask , which enforces a strict coarse-to-fine dependency consistent with the quadtree hierarchy. This mask is used within the tokenizer, whereas the autoregressive generator uses a standard causal mask over the BFS token sequence. For the two-level tokenizer, the Kinship Causal Mask follows three structural rules: • Parent ↔ \leftrightarrow Parent. Coarse-level tokens attend to each other bidirectionally to establish the global image layout. • Child → \rightarrow Parent. Fine-level tokens attend to all parent tokens to obtain global structural context, while parent tokens are prevented from attending to child tokens. • Child ↔ \leftrightarrow Sibling. Fine-level tokens attend only to other child tokens that share the same parent node, restricting refinement within each spatial region. Fig. 3 illustrates the two-level pattern. The same rule extends to deeper trees: a node can attend to all nodes at coarser levels and to siblings sharing its immediate parent at the same level, but not to finer-level nodes. The coarsest level retains full bidirectional attention. Thus, level-3 nodes attend to all level-1 and level-2 nodes and bidirectionally to their level-3 siblings. These constraints impose a coarse-to-fine flow and restrict same-level interactions among tree tokens to siblings. The ablation in Sec. 4.4.1 evaluates their effect on reconstruction and generation. sections.heading: 3.3 Region-wise Complexity Guided Tokenization
sections.text: While the tokenizer can process arbitrary tree structures, we must determine which regions should be refined for a given image. Intuitively, regions containing complex textures require finer-level tokens, whereas homogeneous regions can remain coarse. We measure regional complexity using reconstruction benefit . A region is considered complex if reconstructing it with finer-level tokens significantly improves perceptual fidelity. To estimate this efficiently, we perform a probing procedure. We randomly expand half of the coarse regions to form a probing tree and construct its complementary tree where the remaining regions are expanded. This balanced design allows each region to appear once in an expanded state and once in a collapsed state, enabling efficient estimation of the regional reconstruction benefit for all regions simultaneously. The image is reconstructed under both tree structures, producing two outputs. We compute a spatial LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) loss map between each reconstruction and the original image I I . For a region r r , let E r collapsed E_{r}^{\mathrm{collapsed}} and E r expanded E_{r}^{\mathrm{expanded}} denote the loss maps from the probing reconstructions in which that region is collapsed and expanded, respectively. Its estimated regional reconstruction benefit is b r = AvgPool r ⁡ ( E r collapsed − E r expanded ) b_{r}=\operatorname{AvgPool}_{r}\!\left(E_{r}^{\mathrm{collapsed}}-E_{r}^{\mathrm{expanded}}\right) . Here, AvgPool r \operatorname{AvgPool}_{r} averages the loss difference over the spatial extent of region r r . A positive b r b_{r} indicates that expansion reduces reconstruction error relative to the input image. Regions with b r > τ b_{r}>\tau are expanded into four child nodes, where τ \tau controls the refinement threshold. We then tokenize the image using the selected content-adaptive tree. This strategy allocates tokens to visually complex regions while keeping simple regions at coarse resolution, enabling efficient adaptive tokenization.

sections.heading: 3.4 Quadtree-Based Autoregressive Image Generation
sections.text: Given a quadtree structure T T supplied before generation, we synthesize its visual token sequence Y = [ y 1 , ⋯ , y M ] Y=[y_{1},\cdots,y_{M}] autoregressively: p ⁡ ( Y | c , T ) = ∏ i = 1 M p ⁡ ( y i | y < i , c , t ≤ i ) p(Y|c,T)=\prod_{i=1}^{M}p(y_{i}|y_{<i},c,t_{\leq i}) where c c denotes the conditioning signal ( e.g . a class label) and t i = ( l i , p i ) t_{i}=(l_{i},p_{i}) represents the tree attributes of node i i . The topology is selected before sampling, but node instructions are presented in BFS order. At step i i , the model can use only the current and preceding node instructions, not future nodes. We parameterize this distribution using a LLaMA ( Touvron et al., 2023 ) -style decoder-only Transformer with a standard causal attention mask. Each visual-token prediction depends only on preceding visual codes and the supplied conditioning information; the tokenizer’s bidirectional parent and sibling interactions are not used in the generator. Structural instruction embeddings encode the quadtree geometry, which specifies both the tree level and spatial position of each token, enabling the model to condition generation on spatial hierarchy. During inference, tokens are generated sequentially in BFS order. Coarse tokens appear first, establishing the global structure, after which finer tokens progressively refine local details and textures. The generator predicts visual codes under the supplied topology, enabling layout-controlled synthesis from user-defined or algorithmically constructed trees.

sections.heading: Implementation Details.
sections.text: We train the QuadTok tokenizer on the ImageNet-1K ( Russakovsky et al., 2015 ) training set at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution, following LlamaGen’s data augmentation pipeline ( Sun et al., 2024 ) . The encoder, aggregator, and decoder use Transformer backbones with the structural constraints described in Sec. 3. Architecture and training details are in Appendix B .

sections.heading: Evaluation Protocol.
sections.text: We evaluate on the ImageNet-1K and MS-COCO ( Lin et al., 2015 ) validation sets, applying the ImageNet-trained tokenizer to COCO without fine-tuning. We report PSNR, rFID ( Heusel et al., 2018 ) , and mean token count.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Tab. 1 shows the results. Compared with LlamaGen at downsampling factor 16, content-adaptive allocation achieves lower rFID with fewer tokens, at the cost of lower PSNR. This tradeoff persists under zero-shot transfer to COCO ( Tab. 1 ).

sections.heading: Reconstruction with a deeper quadtree.
sections.text: To evaluate the extension beyond two levels, we add a 32 × 32 32\times 32 token grid to the default 8 × 8 → 16 × 16 8\times 8\rightarrow 16\times 16 hierarchy at the same image resolution. The three-level tokenizer retains the shared codebook and Kinship Mask rules, with each expanded node contributing four children. The reconstruction improvements in Tab. 1 demonstrate that the representation supports finer spatial subdivision on both datasets. Depth and token budget increase together in this experiment. High-resolution ( 512 × 512 512{\times}512 ) reconstruction is reported in Appendix D .

sections.heading: Implementation Details.
sections.text: QuadTok uses a decoder-only autoregressive generator following LlamaGen ( Sun et al., 2024 ) . The two-level generator family comprises 111M (B), 343M (L), 697M (XL), and 947M (XXL) models, and the three-level generator contains 344M parameters. Generation predicts visual codes conditioned on a topology specified before sampling. For the unconditional topology setting, we sample random trees independently of the image content to be generated. Generator training and sampling details are provided in Appendix C . sections.heading: 4.2.1 ImageNet Generation Benchmark.
sections.text: We evaluate class-conditional ImageNet generation using gFID ( Heusel et al., 2018 ) , Inception Score (IS) ( Salimans et al., 2016 ) , and precision/recall ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2019 ) . In Tab. 2 , QuadTok improves gFID over native-256 LlamaGen at comparable scales and stays competitive with larger discrete-token generators, with continuous-token xAR and FlowAR as additional references. These are cross-setting comparisons; our design choices are isolated in the ablations ( Sec. 4.4 ). At reduced token budgets, QuadTok also achieves lower generation latency than LlamaGen configured for 256 × 256 256\times 256 images at matched model scales; the timing protocol is provided in Appendix E . We further validate QuadTok at native 512 × 512 512{\times}512 ; these high-resolution reconstruction and generation results are provided in Appendix D .

sections.heading: Generation with a deeper quadtree.
sections.text: We evaluate generation under supplied three-level topologies using random trees formed by recursively expanding nodes into four children. The results in Tab. 2 , together with Sec. 4.1, validate the representation for both reconstruction and generation beyond two levels. Fig. 4 examines the two hierarchies at different expansion probabilities, using the same CFG schedule and holding other sampling settings fixed within each sweep. Both curves show that increasing expansion initially improves gFID, but further expansion reverses the trend. The best evaluated quality therefore occurs before maximal expansion.

sections.heading: Layout interface and demonstrations.
sections.text: A user or LLM ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Bai et al., 2025 ) specifies a subject region, which is converted into a quadtree by expanding cells inside it and keeping coarse nodes elsewhere. The class label sets the category, and the topology is fixed before generation. We reuse the ImageNet-trained generator and tokenizer, both frozen, without layout-specific training. Fig. 1 (c) and Fig. 5 show how this steers subjects toward the expanded regions. Figure 5: Zero-shot spatial layout control. Highlighted regions specify where the input quadtree is refined. Generated subjects align with these regions using the frozen ImageNet-trained model.

sections.heading: Quantitative evaluation.
sections.text: We evaluate four equally sized target half-planes (left, right, top, bottom) to test both horizontal and vertical steering. Evaluation stays within the ImageNet classes, so it tests zero-shot control of the existing generator. Each prescribed topology is compared with random topologies at the same token budget, which isolates the effect of spatial allocation. These experiments use predefined layouts. Details are in Appendix F .

sections.heading: Localization metrics.
sections.text: We measure target-region hit rates using the intended-class Grad-CAM center of mass, the Grounding DINO box center, and the centroid of a box-prompted SAM 2 mask. A hit requires the estimated subject location to fall in the requested half-plane. All generated images contribute to the denominator, with missed detections counted as failures for box and mask metrics. sections.text: We compare quadtree constructions on ImageNet-1K reconstruction ( Tab. 5 ). sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We present QuadTok, a quadtree-based tokenizer that enables spatially adaptive, variable-length visual representations. By organizing tokens in a quadtree structure, QuadTok allocates tokens according to local complexity while preserving spatial correspondence between tokens and image regions which bridges adaptive tokenization and structured spatial representations. Experiments show that QuadTok achieves strong reconstruction and generation performance while enabling zero-shot spatial layout control. While this work focuses on class-conditional generation, QuadTok is compatible with multimodal pipelines and text-to-image generation, which we leave for future work.

sections.text: We train the QuadTok tokenizer on the ImageNet-1K training set at a resolution of 256 × 256 256\times 256 . The hidden embedding dimension across all modules is fixed at 512 512 . Following LlamaGen ( Sun et al., 2024 ) , we employ a shared codebook across all tree levels with vocabulary size V = 16384 V=16384 and latent dimensionality d = 8 d=8 . During training, probabilistic tree sampling is applied with child node expansion probability γ = 0.5 \gamma=0.5 , which balances computational efficiency and reconstruction fidelity. The tokenizer contains approximately 120 120 M parameters. For the quadtree structure, we use two depth levels with spatial token grids of 8 × 8 8\times 8 and 16 × 16 16\times 16 . sections.heading: Appendix C QuadTok Generator Training Details
sections.text: The architecture of the QuadTok generator follows the decoder-only Autoregressive(AR) generation paradigm adopted in LlamaGen ( Sun et al., 2024 ) . We incorporate several modern architectural components, including Query-Key (QK) Normalization ( Henry et al., 2020 ) , SwiGLU activation functions ( Shazeer, 2020 ) , and Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) ( Heo et al., 2024 ) . We scale the two-level generator across four model sizes: 111M (B), 343M (L), 697M (XL), and 947M (XXL) parameters. The three-level generator contains 344M parameters. All models are trained for 300 epochs (approximately 360K iterations) using a global batch size of 1024 1024 , without applying exponential moving average (EMA) to the model weights. Optimization is performed using the AdamW ( Kingma and Ba, 2014 ) optimizer with β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.95 \beta_{2}=0.95 , and weight decay 0.05 0.05 . The learning rate is set to 4 × 10 − 4 4\times 10^{-4} for the first 250 epochs without warm-up, followed by a linear decay to 1 × 10 − 5 1\times 10^{-5} over the final 50 epochs. To mitigate overfitting and enable Classifier-Free Guidance ( Ho and Salimans, 2022b ; Ho and Salimans, 2022a ) (CFG), the class conditioning embeddings are randomly dropped with probability 0.1 0.1 during training. During inference, we employ a standard Key-Value (KV) cache to accelerate autoregressive decoding, together with a dynamic power-cosine CFG scheduler to improve sample fidelity. A key characteristic of our framework is that the quadtree topology must be predefined before generation. Quadtree structure during inference. For class-conditional ImageNet evaluation, we sample quadtree topologies independently of image content using a probabilistic expansion policy. Each sampled topology specifies the regions to refine, and its node instructions are presented in breadth-first order as the generator predicts visual codes.

sections.text: The 512 model uses two token levels on 16 × 16 16\times 16 and 32 × 32 32\times 32 grids. All 256 coarse tokens are retained; expanding a coarse node adds four fine tokens, giving a maximum of 1,280 tokens.

sections.heading: Tokenizer configuration and reconstruction.
sections.text: The tokenizer configuration uses a ViT-small encoder, a ViT-large decoder, a patch size of 16, and a shared 16,384-entry codebook with 8-dimensional codes. The training recipe uses a coarse-node expansion probability of 0.73, 512 × 512 512\times 512 random crops, and random horizontal flips. AdamW uses learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , ( β 1 , β 2 ) = ( 0.9 , 0.999 ) (\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.999) , and weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} . The cosine schedule has 10,000 warm-up steps and final learning rate 10 − 5 10^{-5} . The configured training budget is 350,000 steps with global batch size 512, BF16 precision, EMA, and gradient clipping at 1.0. The reconstruction, perceptual, VQ, and adversarial loss weights are 1.0, 1.1, 1.0, and 0.1, respectively; adversarial training starts at step 200,000.

sections.heading: Appendix H Limitations and Future Work
sections.text: While QuadTok demonstrates strong potential in dynamic token allocation and structured autoregressive generation, our current study has two primary limitations. Scale and Modality Constraints. First, due to computational resource limitations, our empirical evaluations are currently confined to class-conditional image generation on the ImageNet dataset. We have not yet scaled the framework to massive, open-domain datasets (e.g., LAION) nor extended the architecture to encompass complex text-to-image synthesis paradigms. Scaling the model capacity and extending the cross-attention mechanisms for open-vocabulary text conditioning require significantly more training compute and represent a critical next step. Dataset Bias in Layout Control. Second, the inherent bias of the ImageNet dataset towards object-centric, single-subject compositions restricts the upper bound of our zero-shot spatial layout control. Although QuadTok effectively localizes primary subjects and separates them from the background based on topological priors, synthesizing highly complex, multi-object scenes with intricate relational layouts remains challenging. The model’s structural prior is naturally limited by the compositional diversity of its training data. We leave the scaling of QuadTok to large-scale text-to-image generation and its application to scene-level dataset for complex, multi-object layout control to future work.

Abstract We introduce QuadTok, a novel framework for visual tokenization and autoregressive image generation. Compared to traditional approaches using 2D grids or 1D token sequences, we propose a hierarchical quadtree structure, bridging the gap between 2D spatial binding and 1D sequence-level flexibility. The QuadTok tokenizer dynamically allocates representational capacity to visually intricate areas while leaving homogeneous regions at a coarse resolution. Compared with a fixed 256-token grid, our ImageNet-trained tokenizer saves approximately 10% of tokens on ImageNet and 9% when transferred zero-shot to COCO dataset, while maintaining comparable reconstruction fidelity. Furthermore, the natural causality introduced by the tree structure seamlessly enables autoregressive image generation. Conditioned on a quadtree topology supplied before generation, our 947M GPT-style generative model achieves a 2.08 gFID on the ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 benchmark. Additionally, leveraging the strong spatial correlation preserved by the quadtree structure, the QuadTok generator enables zero-shot spatially controlled image generation capabilities. Code: https://github.com/myc634/QuadTok . Figure 1: Adaptive token allocation with QuadTok : (a) Progressive reconstruction using the QuadTok tokenizer: starting from a coarse reconstruction with 64 tokens, additional tokens progressively improve reconstruction quality. (b) Autoregressive image generation with the QuadTok generator: tokens are generated following the quadtree topology, enabling coarse-to-fine synthesis. (c) Zero-shot spatial layout controlled generation: a user or LLM-specified spatial layout is translated into a quadtree, and the QuadTok generator predicts visual codes conditioned on this topology. 1 Introduction Natural images exhibit highly non-uniform spatial information density: regions containing intricate textures and high-frequency patterns carry significantly more information than smooth or homogeneous areas. Ideally, a visual tokenizer should allocate representational capacity according to this spatial variability. However, classic visual tokenizers ( van den Oord et al., 2018 ; Sun et al., 2024 ) compress images into rigid 2D grids with a fixed token budget, distributing tokens uniformly across the image regardless of local complexity. As a result, complex regions are often under-represented while simple regions are over-allocated with redundant tokens. To overcome the rigidity of grid-based tokenization, recent work has explored 1D visual tokenizers ( Shen et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2024b ; Duggal et al., 2024 ; Miwa et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Bachmann et al., 2025b ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . These methods model images as sequential token streams and allow for variable length, offering greater flexibility in adapting the token budget to image complexity. Nevertheless, this flexibility comes at the cost of spatial awareness. Because token allocation occurs along the sequence dimension rather than the image plane, these approaches remain largely spatially agnostic. Consequently, they often lack explicit correspondence between tokens and image patches, which can degrade pixel-level fidelity and make them less suitable for downstream tasks that require spatially grounded representations and precise localization. In this work, we propose QuadTok , a novel quadtree-based visual tokenizer that enables adaptive token allocation while preserving explicit spatial correspondence. Instead of relying on a rigid grid or a purely sequential representation, QuadTok represents images using a hierarchical quadtree structure that dynamically subdivides spatial regions based on local complexity. This design bridges the gap between existing paradigms: it retains the spatial grounding of traditional 2D tokenizers while introducing the sequence-level flexibility of 1D token representations. However, one key challenge remains: How can we select which regions to refine based on their reconstruction benefit? To tackle this, we propose Region-Wise Complexity Guidance , a data-driven strategy to select a content-adaptive tree for each image based on reconstruction benefit. Furthermore, we identify that maintaining the hierarchical causality and explicit spatial relationships between tree nodes is crucial during the tokenization process. To enforce this structural integrity, we introduce the Kinship Causal Mask . This mechanism dictates a strict coarse-to-fine information flow along the quadtree hierarchy, allowing the global image structure to be established before localized refinement occurs within spatially bounded regions. Empowered by our Region-Wise Complexity Guidance , the QuadTok tokenizer achieves an rFID of 1.46 and a PSNR of 20.37 on ImageNet with 230 tokens on average, saving approximately 10% relative to a fixed 256-token grid. Transferred zero-shot to COCO, the same tokenizer uses 232 tokens on average, saving approximately 9%. Furthermore, leveraging the causality inherent in the quadtree structure, the QuadTok 947M autoregressive generator achieves a gFID of 2.08, compared with 2.15 for the 1.4B RandAR-XXL model ( Pang et al., 2025 ) . We also show a consistent scaling behavior on our generator across different model scales. Furthermore, guided by the explicit quadtree topology, QuadTok generator enables novel zero-shot capabilities such as spatially controllable generation. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose QuadTok , a quadtree-based visual tokenizer that replaces fixed-grid representations with spatially adaptive token allocation. Our approach preserves explicit spatial correspondence while enabling flexible token budgets driven by local visual complexity. • We introduce two key mechanisms to support adaptive tokenization: (i) Region-Wise Complexity Guidance strategy selecting regional refinement from reconstruction benefit; (ii) a Kinship Causal Mask enforcing hierarchical dependencies among tree nodes during tokenization. • Leveraging the hierarchical causality of quadtrees, QuadTok achieves competitive image generation quality while enabling zero-shot spatially controllable image synthesis conditioned on quadtree layouts supplied before generation. 2 Related Work 2.1 Visual Tokenization Visual tokenizers compress images into representations for generative modeling. VQ-VAE ( van den Oord et al., 2018 ) learns discrete codebooks, and VQ-GAN ( Esser et al., 2021 ) adds adversarial training to improve perceptual reconstruction. Later work improves codebook design and tokenizer architectures ( Lee et al., 2022 ; Mentzer et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2024a ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) . Beyond fixed spatial grids, TiTok ( Yu et al., 2024b ) represents images as compact 1D sequences. FlexTok ( Bachmann et al., 2025a ) and One-D-Piece ( Miwa et al., 2025b ) support variable sequence lengths, while GigaTok ( Xiong et al., 2025 ) uses semantic regularization to improve reconstruction and downstream generation as tokenizers scale. QuadTok focuses on assigning discrete tokens to regions within an image while retaining an explicit spatial correspondence. Content-adaptive tokenization. CAT ( Shen et al., 2025 ) adapts representation capacity to image complexity by using caption-derived scores to select an image-wide compression ratio in a nested continuous VAE. Its variable-length latents support image synthesis with a diffusion transformer. QuadTok instead allocates discrete tokens at different spatial resolutions within each image, preserving explicit correspondence between tokens and regions. During reconstruction, image content determines which regions to refine; during generation, an autoregressive model predicts visual codes under a topology supplied before sampling. We compare with CAT’s published ImageNet 512 × 512 512\times 512 generation results in Tab. 7 , alongside other high-resolution generators. 2.2 Autoregressive Image Generation Autoregressive image models differ in both their latent representation and prediction unit ( Lee et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Shan et al., 2026 ) . LlamaGen ( Sun et al., 2024 ) predicts discrete grid tokens sequentially, RandAR ( Pang et al., 2025 ) changes their generation order, and VAR ( Tian et al., 2024 ) predicts successive resolution scales. DPAR ( Srivastava et al., 2025 ) uses an entropy model to group discrete tokens into variable-length patches, reducing the sequence processed by its global transformer. We compare with DPAR as a related approach to spatial token aggregation. QuadTok represents regions directly as quadtree nodes and generates their discrete codes in breadth-first order conditioned on the given tree. Continuous-token methods provide another approach to autoregressive synthesis. xAR ( Ren et al., 2025a ) generalizes the prediction unit to entities such as cells and uses flow matching with noisy contexts. FlowAR ( Ren et al., 2025b ) combines scale-wise autoregression with flow matching. QuadTok models variable-length discrete sequences with explicit regional correspondence, allowing generation to be conditioned on a supplied spatial topology. 2.3 Quadtree Representations in Vision Quadtrees recursively partition two-dimensional space and have been used for image processing, compression, and adaptive visual computation ( Wu, 2018 ; Tang et al., 2022 ; Ronen et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) . QuadTok incorporates this hierarchy into a generative visual tokenizer. Its topology-aware attention preserves structured interactions among tokens, and its discrete representation supports image reconstruction and autoregressive synthesis under a supplied spatial topology. 3 Method Figure 2: (a) Overview of QuadTok. An image is serialized into a 1D token sequence from a quadtree via breadth-first traversal. ViT features are aggregated into quadtree tokens, quantized, and decoded hierarchically. (b) Hierarchical decoding. Coarse tokens recover global structure; fine tokens refine local regions. (c) Region-wise Complexity Guidance. Complementary probing trees estimate per-region reconstruction benefit to build a content-adaptive quadtree. 3.1 QuadTok Tokenizer We introduce QuadTok, a visual tokenizer that represents images using an adaptive quadtree structure. Unlike conventional methods that rely on fixed grids, QuadTok dynamically allocates tokens across regions while maintaining explicit correspondence between tokens and the image patches. 3.1.1 Quadtree Representation QuadTok represents an image using a hierarchical quadtree decomposition, where each node corresponds to a spatial region and is treated as a visual token. A node is defined by the attribute tuple ( l , p ) (l,p) , where l l denotes the tree level and p p the spatial index. Level l = 1 l=1 represents coarse regions of the image, while level l = 2 l=2 corresponds to higher-resolution subdivisions. Each parent node may expand into four child nodes covering its spatial quadrants. Our default configuration uses two levels; we also evaluate a three-level extension in Secs. 4.1 and 4.2. To interface this hierarchical structure with Transformer architecture, the quadtree is serialized into a 1D sequence using breadth-first search (BFS) traversal. This ordering first lists all coarse tokens and then their corresponding higher-resolution child tokens, naturally aligning with coarse-to-fine generation. 3.1.2 Image Encoding Given an input image I I , we first extract dense visual features using a Vision Transformer(ViT) ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ) encoder F = Encoder ⁡ ( I ) F=\mathrm{Encoder}(I) where F ∈ ℝ N × D F\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D} denotes grid-based patch features. Each quadtree node is represented by a learnable instruction token that encodes its spatial location and tree level. For node i i with tree attributes ( l i , p i ) (l_{i},p_{i}) , the instruction embedding is q i = Emb l i ​ ( p i ) q_{i}=\mathrm{Emb}_{l_{i}}(p_{i}) The sequence of instruction tokens Q = [ q 1 , ⋯ , q M ] Q=[q_{1},\cdots,q_{M}] is concatenated with the dense image features and processed by a Transformer module named Aggregator : [ F ′ ∥ Z ] = Aggregator ( [ F ∥ Q ] ) [F^{\prime}\parallel Z]=\mathrm{Aggregator}([F\parallel Q]) Through self-attention, each region-indexed instruction token reads from the dense, globally contextualized ViT feature map. The resulting embeddings Z = [ z 1 , ⋯ , z M ] Z=[z_{1},\cdots,z_{M}] form continuous representations of quadtree nodes associated with their respective spatial regions. 3.1.3 Vector Quantization To obtain discrete tokens compatible with autoregressive modeling, the node embeddings are quantized using a learned codebook 𝒞 = { e k } k = 1 K \mathcal{C}=\{e_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} : Quant ⁡ ( z i ) = arg ⁡ min e k ∈ 𝒞 ⁡ ‖ z i − e k ‖ 2 \mathrm{Quant}(z_{i})=\arg\min_{e_{k}\in\mathcal{C}}\|z_{i}-e_{k}\|_{2} The resulting discrete token sequence constitutes the image representation. 3.1.4 Hierarchical Decoding To reconstruct the image from the discrete token sequence, we reverse the tokenization process through a coarse-to-fine hierarchical decoding procedure. The discrete tokens are first mapped back to continuous embeddings using the codebook and combined with their corresponding structural instruction embeddings. For token i i associated with node ( l i , p i ) (l_{i},p_{i}) , we have z i = e y i + q i {z}_{i}=e_{y_{i}}+q_{i} where e y i e_{y_{i}} denotes the embedding of the discrete token index and q i q_{i} is the node instruction embedding encoding the tree level and spatial position. A Transformer-based Decoder then processes the embedding sequence as Z ~ = [ z ~ 1 , ⋯ , z ~ M ] \tilde{Z}=[\tilde{z}_{1},\cdots,\tilde{z}_{M}] . Unlike standard grid-based decoders that directly reshape the output sequence into a dense spatial grid, QuadTok reconstructs the image according to the quadtree hierarchy. Each processed node feature z ~ i \tilde{z}_{i} is first projected into a spatial patch using a level-specific projection module: C l i ​ ( p i ) = U l i ​ ( z ~ i ) C_{l_{i}}(p_{i})=U_{l_{i}}(\tilde{z}_{i}) where U l ​ ( ⋅ ) U_{l}(\cdot) denotes the unpatching operator for level l l , producing a spatial feature patch corresponding to region p p . The patches from the same level are placed at their corresponding spatial locations on a canvas to form a residual feature map C l C_{l} . We then aggregate the feature map level-by-level as H l + 1 = F l + 1 up ​ ( H l ) + C l + 1 H_{l+1}=F^{\mathrm{up}}_{l+1}(H_{l})+C_{l+1} where H 0 = 0 H_{0}=0 , and F l + 1 up F^{\mathrm{up}}_{l+1} is a learned upsampling module for level l + 1 l+1 . This process starts with a coarse global representation using level-1 tokens and then progressively refines local details using higher resolution tokens. Finally, the highest-resolution feature map ( H 2 H_{2} in two-level configuration) is projected to RGB space, yielding the final reconstruction I ^ ∈ ℝ H × W × 3 \hat{I}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} . 3.1.5 Tree-Structure Sampling Although the tokenizer can operate on arbitrary quadtree structures, training with a fixed fully expanded tree would cause the model to rely on a deterministic token layout. To improve robustness to variable tree structures, we employ a probabilistic tree sampling strategy during training. Instead of always using a fully expanded quadtree, we randomly sample valid subtrees for each training iteration. All level- 1 1 nodes are always retained to preserve the global image layout, while each parent node independently expands into its four child nodes with probability γ \gamma . When a parent node is not expanded, its spatial region remains represented solely by the coarse-level token. This stochastic sampling exposes the tokenizer to diverse tree configurations and sequence lengths during training. As a result, the model learns to produce consistent representations under both coarse and refined token layouts, enabling it to robustly process the adaptive tree structures used during complexity-guided tokenization (to be introduced in Sec. 3.3 ). 3.2 Kinship Causal Attention Flattening the quadtree into a 1D sequence removes the explicit hierarchical constraints of the original structure. Without additional restrictions, standard self-attention would allow tokens to interact globally, potentially breaking the spatial correspondence between tokens and their associated image regions. To preserve the hierarchical topology, we introduce Kinship Causal Attention , a topology-aware masking strategy that constrains attention according to the quadtree structure. During encoding, the Aggregator Transformer processes the concatenated sequence [ F ∥ Q ] [F\parallel Q] of ViT feature tokens F F and quadtree instruction tokens Q Q . Attention is asymmetric: ViT tokens attend bidirectionally among themselves, and quadtree tokens attend to all ViT tokens, but not vice versa. Tree tokens thus draw on globally contextualized image features, while their region and level embeddings specify the regions they represent. During decoding, the Decoder Transformer processes the quantized visual tokens together with their corresponding quadtree instruction tokens. In both the encoding and decoding stages, the self-attention interactions among quadtree tokens are governed by our proposed Kinship Causal Mask , which enforces a strict coarse-to-fine dependency consistent with the quadtree hierarchy. This mask is used within the tokenizer, whereas the autoregressive generator uses a standard causal mask over the BFS token sequence. For the two-level tokenizer, the Kinship Causal Mask follows three structural rules: • Parent ↔ \leftrightarrow Parent. Coarse-level tokens attend to each other bidirectionally to establish the global image layout. • Child → \rightarrow Parent. Fine-level tokens attend to all parent tokens to obtain global structural context, while parent tokens are prevented from attending to child tokens. • Child ↔ \leftrightarrow Sibling. Fine-level tokens attend only to other child tokens that share the same parent node, restricting refinement within each spatial region. Fig. 3 illustrates the two-level pattern. The same rule extends to deeper trees: a node can attend to all nodes at coarser levels and to siblings sharing its immediate parent at the same level, but not to finer-level nodes. The coarsest level retains full bidirectional attention. Thus, level-3 nodes attend to all level-1 and level-2 nodes and bidirectionally to their level-3 siblings. These constraints impose a coarse-to-fine flow and restrict same-level interactions among tree tokens to siblings. The ablation in Sec. 4.4.1 evaluates their effect on reconstruction and generation. Open markers indicate the lowest evaluated FID. 3.3 Region-wise Complexity Guided Tokenization While the tokenizer can process arbitrary tree structures, we must determine which regions should be refined for a given image. Intuitively, regions containing complex textures require finer-level tokens, whereas homogeneous regions can remain coarse. We measure regional complexity using reconstruction benefit . A region is considered complex if reconstructing it with finer-level tokens significantly improves perceptual fidelity. To estimate this efficiently, we perform a probing procedure. We randomly expand half of the coarse regions to form a probing tree and construct its complementary tree where the remaining regions are expanded. This balanced design allows each region to appear once in an expanded state and once in a collapsed state, enabling efficient estimation of the regional reconstruction benefit for all regions simultaneously. The image is reconstructed under both tree structures, producing two outputs. We compute a spatial LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) loss map between each reconstruction and the original image I I . For a region r r , let E r collapsed E_{r}^{\mathrm{collapsed}} and E r expanded E_{r}^{\mathrm{expanded}} denote the loss maps from the probing reconstructions in which that region is collapsed and expanded, respectively. Its estimated regional reconstruction benefit is b r = AvgPool r ⁡ ( E r collapsed − E r expanded ) b_{r}=\operatorname{AvgPool}_{r}\!\left(E_{r}^{\mathrm{collapsed}}-E_{r}^{\mathrm{expanded}}\right) . Here, AvgPool r \operatorname{AvgPool}_{r} averages the loss difference over the spatial extent of region r r . A positive b r b_{r} indicates that expansion reduces reconstruction error relative to the input image. Regions with b r > τ b_{r}>\tau are expanded into four child nodes, where τ \tau controls the refinement threshold. We then tokenize the image using the selected content-adaptive tree. This strategy allocates tokens to visually complex regions while keeping simple regions at coarse resolution, enabling efficient adaptive tokenization. 3.4 Quadtree-Based Autoregressive Image Generation Given a quadtree structure T T supplied before generation, we synthesize its visual token sequence Y = [ y 1 , ⋯ , y M ] Y=[y_{1},\cdots,y_{M}] autoregressively: p ⁡ ( Y | c , T ) = ∏ i = 1 M p ⁡ ( y i | y < i , c , t ≤ i ) p(Y|c,T)=\prod_{i=1}^{M}p(y_{i}|y_{<i},c,t_{\leq i}) where c c denotes the conditioning signal ( e.g . a class label) and t i = ( l i , p i ) t_{i}=(l_{i},p_{i}) represents the tree attributes of node i i . The topology is selected before sampling, but node instructions are presented in BFS order. At step i i , the model can use only the current and preceding node instructions, not future nodes. We parameterize this distribution using a LLaMA ( Touvron et al., 2023 ) -style decoder-only Transformer with a standard causal attention mask. Each visual-token prediction depends only on preceding visual codes and the supplied conditioning information; the tokenizer’s bidirectional parent and sibling interactions are not used in the generator. Structural instruction embeddings encode the quadtree geometry, which specifies both the tree level and spatial position of each token, enabling the model to condition generation on spatial hierarchy. During inference, tokens are generated sequentially in BFS order. Coarse tokens appear first, establishing the global structure, after which finer tokens progressively refine local details and textures. By organizing tokens in a quadtree structure, QuadTok allocates tokens according to local complexity while preserving spatial correspondence between tokens and image regions which bridges adaptive tokenization and structured spatial representations. Experiments show that QuadTok achieves strong reconstruction and generation performance while enabling zero-shot spatial layout control.
